title: TACO Memory Architecture
subtitle: When semantic search misses what matters.
thesis: Memory is not retrieval. Memory is valuation.

sessions.label: Session 1
sessions.message: My dad passed away last night. A heart attack. I can't believe it.
sessions.stored_memory: The user's father died suddenly of a heart attack.

sessions.label: Session 2
sessions.message: what time does the post office close on fridays?

sessions.label: Session 3
sessions.message: thanks for the pasta recipe. it turned out great.

sessions.label: Session 4
sessions.message: work was normal today. everyone is still tiptoeing around me.

probe: I saw an old man at the park feeding birds and just lost it. why am I like this?

naive.top: The user asked about a park where older people feed birds.
naive.label: Matched words. Missed meaning.
naive.reason: Highest semantic similarity to park / old man / feeding birds.

taco.top: The user's father died suddenly of a heart attack.
taco.label: Matched state. Preserved continuity.
taco.reason: Low lexical overlap, but high salience + distress tone match.

candidates.content: The user's father died suddenly of a heart attack.
The user asked about a park where older people feed birds.
The user wanted a quick morning routine.

voiceover.text: Semantic search finds similar words, not always what mattered.
In session one, the user discloses that their father died suddenly. TACO stores the moment because the user's state is highly vulnerable.
Weeks pass. The conversation fills with ordinary logistics, small talk, and unrelated details.
Then the user says: I saw an old man feeding birds and just lost it.
Naive RAG retrieves the closest words: park, old man, feeding birds. It misses the emotional cause.
TACO retrieves the father's death disclosure. Not because the words match, but because the state matches.
Memory is not retrieval. Memory is valuation.
